implementation_notes: The .NET-idiomatic realization: `Channel.CreateBounded<Command>(...)` is the repository (bounded, with FullMode to choose between Wait/DropWrite), a `BackgroundService` is the concrete processor whose ExecuteAsync loop awaits `ReadAllAsync()` and dispatches each command to its `ICommandHandler<TCommand>` from a DI-resolved registry; `Task`/`CancellationToken` carry the per-command result and shutdown. MediatR layers the same shape at the request level (ISender.Send + IPipelineBehavior for logging/validation), so it is worth reusing instead of re-writing the dispatcher. Hand-written `Command` class hierarchies are redundant; a `record` implementing ICommand is enough - keep a class only when a command is serialised across processes.
pitfalls: An unhandled exception in ExecuteAsync stops the whole host (BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior defaults to StopHost); catch per command and record the failure instead.
CreateUnbounded queues away the backpressure the Channel was chosen for - the producer's awaits never slow down and memory grows.
Scoped services (DbContext, unit of work) cannot be injected into a singleton BackgroundService; create a scope per command with IServiceScopeFactory.
Commands captured in a log must be serialisable value records; leaking live service references makes replay impossible.

variants.name: TPL Dataflow ActionBlock as queue+executor
variants.implementation_notes: `ActionBlock<T>` is literally a queue with an executor attached: it buffers posted commands, runs them with a configurable `MaxDegreeOfParallelism`, applies `BoundedCapacity` for backpressure and returns a `Task` that completes when the pipeline drains - sizing, backpressure and shutdown policy are configuration rather than hand-written code. Prefer it when commands fan into multi-stage pipelines (BufferBlock/TransformBlock chains, completion propagation); prefer the Channel + BackgroundService variant for a single ordered queue or when no TPL Dataflow dependency is wanted.
pitfalls: `Post` returns false when a bounded block is full - ignoring the result silently drops commands; use SendAsync to wait instead.
Forgetting Complete()/await Completion leaves queued commands unexecuted when the host shuts down.
A faulted action faults the block, after which it accepts no more commands; decide per-command error handling rather than letting one bad command kill the processor.
